entry.lemma: the Zion-pilgrimage oracle shared by Isaiah and Micah
entry.partOfSpeech: convention: shared rendering of a parallel passage across two books
entry.standardEnglish: ASV renders the two passages in nearly identical English; NRSV and NJPS likewise harmonise the shared clauses
entry.wohChoice: One English wording for the clauses Isa 2:2-4 and Mic 4:1-3 share, fixed at isaiah-woh 2:2-4: 'And it shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of YHWH shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and … shall flow to it. And many … shall go and say: “Come, and let us go up to the mountain of YHWH, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us of his ways, and that we may walk in his paths.” For out of Zion shall go forth teaching, and the word of YHWH from Jerusalem. And he shall judge between …, and shall decide for …; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any more.' Where the Hebrew of Micah differs (Mic 4:1 word order, ʿammîm 'peoples', the added hûʾ in wᵉnissāʾ hûʾ miggᵉḇāʿôṯ, and ʿālāyw 'upon it' for Isaiah's ʾēlāyw 'to it'; Mic 4:2 wᵉʾel-bêt 'and to the house' for Isaiah's ʾel-bêt; Mic 4:2 gôyim rabbîm 'many nations'; 4:3 'between many peoples … for strong nations afar off'; the plural yiśʾû; Mic 4:4-5 without Isaiah parallel), the micah-woh line follows Micah's own Hebrew in the same vocabulary.
entry.rationale: Isa 2:2-4 and Mic 4:1-3 are the longest verbatim parallel between two prophetic books, and the scholarly consensus treats them as one oracle transmitted in two collections, whatever the direction of dependence (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, 1991; Williamson, Isaiah 1-5, ICC, 2006; Hillers, Micah, Hermeneia, 1984; Andersen and Freedman, Micah, AB 24E, 2000). A reader comparing the two books should see identical English where the Hebrew is identical and different English only where the Hebrew differs, so the shared clauses are fixed once. isaiah-woh is translated first (micah-woh has no chapter 4 yet), and its Editor-approved wording becomes the reference; the lexical decisions inside it are governed by be-acharit-ha-yamim-latter-days-temporal-eschatological-horizon-cross-corpus ('in the latter days'), torah-teaching-isaiah ('teaching'; the micah-woh Editor should extend or mirror it), elohei-yisrael-god-of-israel-isaiah-24 ('the God of Jacob'), and lexical-cruxes-isaiah-2 ('on the top of', 'flow', 'decide for', 'plowshares'). The convention is descriptive of the texts and carries no lens. Isa 2:5 is not governed: Mic 4:5 has no parallel to it. The micah-woh Editor should render Mic 4:1 ʿālāyw and 4:2 wᵉʾel-bêt from Micah's own Hebrew and not carry Isaiah's 'to it' / 'to the house' across unexamined. The Micah refIds are prospective and become live when micah-woh chapter 4 is drafted.

entry.partOfSpeech: verb (Poel participle, used as a noun)
entry.standardEnglish: soothsayer(s) (ASV Isa 2:6; Mic 5:12 [MT 5:11]); observer of times (KJV Deut 18:10); one who practises augury / soothsaying (NRSV)
entry.wohChoice: 'soothsayer(s)' for the Poel of ʿnn (Isa 2:6 'and are soothsayers like the Philistines'; Mic 5:11 'you shall have no soothsayers'), as a general term for a forbidden divinatory practice; no derivation is built into the English.
entry.rationale: The Poel of ʿnn names one of the divinatory practices forbidden in Israel (Lev 19:26; Deut 18:10, 14; 2 Kgs 21:6 // 2 Chr 33:6; Isa 2:6; 57:3; Jer 27:9; Mic 5:11). Its derivation is unknown: proposals include ʿānān 'cloud' (reading signs in the clouds), an onomatopoeic root for humming or crooning, and a link with ʿayin 'eye' (BDB; HALOT; Jeffers, Magic and Divination in Ancient Palestine and Syria, 1996; Cryer, Divination in Ancient Israel and its Near Eastern Environment, JSOTSup 142, 1994). Because none is established, the project renders the standard general term 'soothsayer', already printed at micah-woh 5:11, and keeps one English word across the corpus so readers can trace the practice. The cloud derivation is lens-salient (it would make the practice one of observing the sky); it is reported only in labelled commentary and is not adopted in any line. The claim is direct because 'soothsayer' is the standard rendering and carries no interpretive choice beyond the lexica.

entry.standardEnglish: idols (ASV, NRSV, NJPS); KJV also "things of nought"
entry.wohChoice: 'idols' for the plural ʾĕlîlîm (Isa 2:8, 18, 20; later 10:10-11; 19:1, 3; 31:7; Lev 19:4; 26:1; Ps 96:5), with the sound-play on ʾēl / ʾĕlōhîm and the sense 'nothings' carried in commentary; the adjective ʾĕlîl 'worthless' (Job 13:4; Zech 11:17) is rendered by its sense.
entry.rationale: ʾĕlîlîm is the polemical word for the images and gods of other peoples, frequent in Isaiah (2:8, 18, 20; 10:10-11; 19:1, 3; 31:7) and attested in the Torah (Lev 19:4; 26:1) and the Psalms (Ps 96:5 // 1 Chr 16:26, 'all the gods of the peoples are ʾĕlîlîm'). It is generally connected with the adjective ʾĕlîl 'worthless, nothing' and is felt as a deliberate distortion of ʾēl / ʾĕlōhîm (BDB; HALOT; Preuss, TDOT 1:285-287), and Isa 2:18 adds a pun with kālîl 'wholly'. The standard English versions render 'idols', and the project keeps that rendering in the line, because 'nothings' or 'worthless gods' would turn a noun into a gloss and lose the noun's ordinary reference to cult images. The wordplay is recorded in commentary wherever it is exploited. No existing central entry governs the lemma (pesel-utemunah governs pesel 'carved image'), so the entry keeps one English word for ʾĕlîlîm across the corpus. The claim is direct: it is the consensus rendering.
